solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Again take up painting after a break

indicators.note: one piece is placed after the other, so the word for the break comes first in the answer

blocks.note: a rest is a break from activity
painting is a form of art

explanation.surface: An artist returns to the easel after time off.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists painting first, but 'after' puts the break at the front of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To restart something is to begin it once more after stopping, the same as resuming an activity.

clue.text: Rub out the L in “articulate”

indicators.note: one thing placed in another means a letter goes inside the word for speaking clearly

blocks.note: the letter itself
to articulate is to say or utter

explanation.surface: An instruction to erase a letter L written within a word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rub out' looks like an instruction to delete, and 'articulate' like a word to search; in fact the L goes into SAY to give SLAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Rub out is slang for murder, and to slay is to kill violently.

clue.text: Champ at the bit, about to go away

indicators.note: about means going round, so the word for the small piece wraps around the word for munching

blocks.note: to champ is to chew or eat noisily
taken as written

explanation.surface: An impatient horse champing at the bit, ready to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Champ at the bit' reads as one idiom, but Champ and bit are separate pieces: B(EAT)IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Beat it is an informal imperative telling someone to leave, matching an order to go away.

clue.text: Give her a turn – a bad scare – in the investigation

indicators.note: giving something a turn rotates and rearranges it, so the pronoun is mixed up
something gone bad is spoilt and out of shape, so the fright word is jumbled too

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone frightens a woman badly during an inquiry.
explanation.walkthrough: The two short words of fodder are scrambled together; 'Give' and 'a' only dress the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Research is systematic study or inquiry, which is what an investigation is.

clue.text: If all else fails, that rickety tower’s to be demolished

indicators.note: a rickety structure is shaky and falling apart, so these letters come apart and are rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: As a last resort, a crumbling tower will have to be knocked down.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means in the most unfavourable outcome, a fallback when every better option has failed.

clue.text: Smuggle the king through in nun disguise? Forget it!

indicators.note: a disguise changes appearance, so the letters of the religious woman are rearranged
smuggling something through means hiding it inside, so the monarch goes within the other letters

blocks.note: taken as written
King Lear of Shakespeare's tragedy

explanation.surface: A plot to sneak a monarch out dressed as a nun, abandoned with a shrug.
explanation.walkthrough: Lear is the crossword's favourite king; NUN is shuffled to UNN and LEAR slips in: UN(LEAR)N.
explanation.definitionFit: To unlearn is to discard knowledge or habits deliberately, that is, to put them out of mind.

clue.text: Wrote back “The material was misleading”

blocks.note: rep is a ribbed fabric used for upholstery
lied means told untruths

explanation.surface: A reply letter complaining that the fabric was not as advertised.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted sentence looks like the content of the reply; it is REP + LIED.
explanation.definitionFit: To reply is to answer, and a written response sent to a correspondent is writing back.

clue.text: Reject and it’s sent back, enclosed – just one’s luck

indicators.note: sent back means returned, so the short word with an apostrophe is read backwards
enclosed means held inside, so the turned word goes within the refusal word

blocks.note: to deny is to refuse or reject
taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A rejected letter returned with its enclosure: just my luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just one's luck' reads as a grumble, but it is the definition; the apostrophe in it's is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: Destiny is the fate allotted to a person, the fortune that happens to befall them.

clue.text: Has a job, but does prevent from skating?

blocks.note: first meaning: occupies an official post
second meaning, split into three: keeps people back from the frozen rink surface

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as HOLDS OFF + ICE: one who holds people off the ice stops them skating.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who holds office occupies a formal position, so they are in employment of a sort.

clue.text: One of the in people

blocks.note: surface reading: a member of the fashionable, trendy set
setter's reading: someone who is literally in, at their own house, rather than out

explanation.walkthrough: 'In' means fashionable on the surface, but here it means simply indoors.
explanation.definitionFit: A homebody who rarely goes out is always in, the opposite of a socialite.

clue.text: Tip “Bad Boy”

blocks.note: first meaning: of a ship, lean over to one side
second meaning: a cad, a dishonourable man

explanation.surface: Advice about a rogue, as if a tip-off on a villain.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship heels when it tilts in the wind, and a heel is an old word for a scoundrel.

clue.text: Believed to have quoted a revolutionary in

indicators.note: placed in means put inside, so the revolutionary goes within the word for quoted

blocks.note: to cite is to quote
red is a common term for a communist or revolutionary

explanation.surface: Someone thought to have quoted a revolutionary figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Red for a communist comes from the red flag of revolution.
explanation.definitionFit: To credit a story is to accept it as true, so credited means trusted as being true.

clue.text: Is useless and not a philanthropist

blocks.note: first meaning: has no beneficial effect
second meaning, read literally: someone who performs no charitable deeds

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense plays on do-gooder: a person who never helps others literally does no good.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes something ineffective, and also a person who never performs benevolent acts.

clue.text: In return, the artist gets compensation for

indicators.note: in return suggests turning back, so the word for the artist is read from the end

blocks.note: one who draws pictures

explanation.surface: An artist is paid in exchange for their work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In return' looks like part of the payment idea, but it signals the reversal of DRAWER.
explanation.definitionFit: A reward is something given in recognition of service, a payment or recompense.

clue.text: Is unsuccessful in one’s attempt to go places?

definitions.text: in one’s attempt to go places?

blocks.note: first meaning: makes no progress

blocks.clueFragment: in one’s attempt to go places?
blocks.note: second meaning, read literally: a traveller who sets off and reaches no destination at all

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go places' is an idiom for success; taken literally, failing to reach any place is the phrase for failure.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means making no progress, unable to achieve anything despite effort.

clue.text: Anxious to give up sweets

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is written from bottom to top, so it runs backwards

blocks.note: desserts are sweet courses, called sweets in Britain

explanation.surface: Someone nervous about giving up sugary treats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give up' looks like quitting a habit; 'up' alone signals the reversal. In Britain the pudding course is called sweets.
explanation.definitionFit: Being stressed means under nervous strain, a state of worry close to anxiety.

clue.text: Rests before a night on the tiles?

definitions.text: Rests before a night on the tiles?

blocks.note: surface reading: a night out partying, which people prepare for with a sleep
setter's reading: the short sleeps cats take before prowling the rooftops at night

explanation.walkthrough: A night on the tiles is British slang for a wild night out, originally from cats roaming the roofs.
explanation.definitionFit: Short daytime dozes are named after cats, which famously sleep by day and go out at night.

clue.text: Looks to find the broken legs trapped can, if moved

indicators.note: broken limbs are out of shape, so the letters of these limbs are rearranged
moved means shifted about, so the letters of the tin are rearranged too
trapped means held inside, so the shifted tin sits within the shifted limbs

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grim scene: broken legs pinned by a can that has shifted.
explanation.definitionFit: Glances are quick looks, brief glimpses cast at something.

clue.text: The way to pronounce “demesne”

indicators.note: pronouncing a word means saying it, so the answer is matched to its spoken sound

blocks.note: a demesne is an estate, a lord's manor

explanation.surface: A pronunciation guide for the tricky word demesne.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a guide to saying demesne (pronounced 'di-MAIN'); in fact demesne means a manor, which sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A manner is a method or fashion of doing something, the way it is done.

clue.text: Got a folder out to put in, as you anticipated

indicators.note: out suggests something put out of order, so the letters of the file holder are rearranged
put in means placed inside, so the small word goes within the rearranged letters

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An office scene: someone took out a folder to file, just as predicted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got a' and 'as you' only dress the surface; the inserted word is the plain 'to' in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Foretold means predicted in advance, so something foretold was expected or anticipated.

clue.text: Prattles about how it’s powered by

blocks.note: first meaning: talks on and on without stopping
second meaning: uses as fuel, as an engine does petrol

explanation.surface: Someone babbling on about how a machine works.
explanation.definitionFit: A chatterer keeps talking endlessly, and a machine is driven by whatever fuel it consumes.

clue.text: Catch on there’s something wrong

blocks.note: first meaning: a hidden drawback or problem
second meaning: an unexpected hitch or obstacle

explanation.surface: Someone suddenly realising that a thing is amiss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch on' reads as one phrase meaning understand, but 'on' only links the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A snag is a hidden difficulty or hitch, the catch in a deal that means a problem exists.

clue.text: Used the time to get assistance

blocks.note: a second is a unit of time
to give a hand is to help

explanation.surface: Someone spent time to obtain help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used' looks like a verb but the definition is the adjective meaning not new.
explanation.definitionFit: Second-hand goods have been owned before, so they are pre-owned rather than new.

clue.text: Animal fur must be declared

indicators.note: declared means spoken out, so the answer is the spoken sound of the word for fur

blocks.note: fur is an animal's hair

explanation.surface: A customs officer insisting that animal furs be declared.
explanation.definitionFit: The hare is a fast long-eared mammal, so it is an example of an animal.

clue.text: “Fish pie? Pish, fie!” he said!

blocks.note: surface reading: someone sneering at a fish pie with old-fashioned scorn
setter's reading: the reply swaps the first sounds of the two words, the slip named after an Oxford don

explanation.walkthrough: The quoted retort is itself a spoonerism of 'fish pie'; William Spooner, an Oxford don, was famed for such swaps of initial sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue quotes a typical transposition, so the speaker is the man whose name is given to such slips.

clue.text: Lived in, though it’s shut up

blocks.note: first meaning: lodged as a paying guest
second meaning: covered with planks, as an empty house

explanation.surface: A house that is occupied even though it looks closed.
explanation.definitionFit: A boarder lodges in a house, and a derelict building is covered over with wooden planks.
